passage:
Sit, Nirmala. Your Urmila Nani will tell you about the summer she was twenty.
A boy called Devesh from the next lane began sending letters through my brother every single day. Beautiful letters. By the second week he wrote that we should marry before the rains. My heart was racing, I won't lie. But my Amma had taught me one thing: fast rivers carry mud.
So I wrote back only this: "I like your letters. I want to know you slowly. I will still go to my sewing class, and to Saroj's house on Thursdays."
Then I waited to see what he would do. His next letter came four days later, not one. It said: "Take all the time you need. Tell me what you are stitching."
That letter, beta, is the reason I said yes a year later. Your Nana still asks me what I am stitching.

qa.q: What did Devesh write in the second week?
qa.a: He wrote that they should marry before the rains.

qa.q: How was young Urmila feeling when the marriage letter came?
qa.a: Her heart was racing with excitement, yet she felt cautious, remembering her Amma's saying that fast rivers carry mud.

qa.q: Why was young Urmila's reply to Devesh a wise turning point in the story?
qa.a: She said she liked him but kept her sewing class and Thursdays at Saroj's house, which slowed things without ending them and let her see how Devesh treated a gentle no.

qa.q: How might Devesh have felt when her slow reply arrived?
qa.a: He may have felt a little disappointed, but his warm letter asking what she was stitching shows he respected her pace and was curious about her life.

grounding: A grandmother recalls slowing a fast courtship at twenty, keeping her own routines, and trusting the suitor who stayed warm when she asked for time.

passage:
Yamini had three exams in five days and a phone that would not stop glowing. Rashmi, whom she had met at a college hackathon barely three weeks earlier, had booked two bus seats to the hills for Friday. "Surprise! Our first trip," the message said, followed by a row of hearts.
Yamini sat on the hostel stairs, notes on her knees, and typed slowly. "That's sweet. But I'm not ready for a trip, and this week I need to study and meet my study group. Dinner after exams?"
She put the phone face down and read one full chapter before turning it over.
Three missed calls. Then: "Wow. I planned everything for you. Fine." Then nothing for a whole day.
Yamini noticed her hands were cold. She also noticed that her answer had been kind, and that the kindness had been met with a door slammed shut. She kept studying, and on Wednesday she told her roommate what had happened.

qa.q: How many exams did Yamini have that week?
qa.a: Yamini had three exams in five days.

qa.q: What do Yamini's cold hands suggest about how she felt after Rashmi's reply?
qa.a: She felt anxious and shaken, because her gentle answer had been met with sulking and silence.

qa.q: Which of Yamini's choices protected her, and why?
qa.a: Reading a full chapter before checking the phone, keeping her study group, and telling her roommate kept her own routine and people close, so the silence could not push her into giving in.

qa.q: What would change if Rashmi had replied warmly to the idea of dinner after exams?
qa.a: Yamini would feel safe slowing down, and the warm reply would show respect for her time; instead the cold "Fine" was a warning sign.

grounding: A student slows a three-week-old romance during exam week, keeps her routines and people, and notices that Rashmi turns cold at a gentle no.

passage:
On the fifth evening they'd spent together, over masala dosa at a crowded café in Pune, Naveen said, "My parents are visiting next week. I want you to meet them."
Farida put down her spoon. She liked him. She liked him a lot. And that was exactly why she wanted to go slowly.
"Naveen, I really like this. But I'd like more time before meeting family. And I'm still doing my Sunday badminton with the girls, and my Thursday class. I don't want to drop those."
She watched his face. This was the moment she'd been told to watch.
Naveen nodded. "That makes sense. I got excited." He smiled. "Can I come watch badminton sometime? From the stands, silently?"
Farida laughed. "Maybe in a month."
"Deal."
Walking home, she felt something she hadn't expected: calmer, and more interested in him, not less.

qa.q: What does Farida do on Sundays?
qa.a: She does her Sunday badminton with the girls.

qa.q: How did Farida feel walking home?
qa.a: Farida felt calmer and more interested in Naveen, because he stayed warm when she slowed things down.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Farida asked for time and kept her routines, then watched Naveen's reaction; his warm acceptance showed he could respect her pace.

qa.q: How does Naveen react to Farida's request?
qa.a: Naveen feels a little sheepish about getting excited, but stays warm and jokes about watching from the stands.

grounding: It shows a young adult asking for time, keeping friends and routines, and watching a new partner stay warm when she slows the pace.

passage:
"Wasim, I need to say something." Tanuja pulled her dupatta tighter on the bench outside the library. "You've messaged me all day, every day, for two weeks. I like you. But I need to slow down."
"Slow down? I thought you felt the same."
"I do like you. I also want time with my friends. I'm going to my cousin's on Saturday."
"Saturday was our plan."
"We didn't plan it. You did."
He looked away. "Fine. I guess I care more than you."
Tanuja noticed her stomach tighten. That sentence again. The second time this week.
"That's not fair, Wasim."
"Whatever. Go to your cousin's."
He walked off. Tanuja sat alone for a while. Then she called her cousin. "I'll be there Saturday. Can I talk to you about something?"
It hurt. But she had learned something important from a single gentle no.

qa.q: Where was Tanuja going on Saturday?
qa.a: She was going to her cousin's.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel when Wasim said he cared more than her?
qa.a: Tanuja felt a tight, uneasy feeling in her stomach, recognising the guilt-heavy line from earlier in the week.

qa.q: What did Tanuja do that protected herself?
qa.a: She kept her plans, named the unfair comment calmly, and reached out to her cousin to talk it through.

qa.q: What does Wasim's reaction reveal?
qa.a: Wasim's cold, sulking reply to a gentle no suggests he struggles to respect her pace, which is useful for Tanuja to know early.

grounding: It shows a young adult asking for time and keeping her plans, and learning something important from how a new partner reacts to a gentle no.

passage:
I'm Pema, and three weeks after I met Chaitanya, I did something I'd never done before: I asked for slowness.
He was wonderful. He was also everywhere. Morning messages, evening calls, a gift on the tenth day. My friends were starting to tease me that I'd vanished.
So one night I said it: "I really like you. But I want to keep my Tuesday football and my weekends with my friends. Can we see each other two evenings a week for now?"
I braced myself. Sulking? A guilt trip? Silence?
Chaitanya just said, "Okay. That's fair. Tell me which two evenings." Then he asked how my football team was doing.
That's when I trusted him more. Not because of the gifts or the messages. Because when I said slow down, he didn't get cold. He just got curious.
We still see each other two evenings a week. It's been a year.

qa.q: On which day did Chaitanya give a gift?
qa.a: A gift on the tenth day.

qa.q: How did Pema feel after Chaitanya's reply?
qa.a: Pema felt relieved and more trusting, because he stayed warm and curious instead of sulking.

qa.q: What did Pema do that was wise?
qa.a: Pema asked for a slower pace, kept football and friends, and watched how Chaitanya reacted to the gentle no.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya seem to see Pema's request?
qa.a: Chaitanya sees it as fair and reasonable, simply asking which evenings and showing interest in Pema's football.

grounding: It shows a young adult asking for time and keeping routines, and trusting a new partner more because he stays warm when the pace slows.

passage:
Counselling note, college wellbeing centre, Tuesday.
Parveen, second year, came in for a follow-up. Three weeks ago she told me that Chinmay, whom she met at a debate meet, wanted to "make it official" after four days and was calling late every night. Today she described what she has tried since. She told him she likes him and wants to go slower. She kept her Saturday badminton with her hostel friends and her weekly call home. She said she is watching how he takes a gentle no.
His reaction, as she reports it: at first he went quiet for a day, then said he understood and asked if Sunday lunch still worked. Parveen laughed as she told me this, and her shoulders looked less raised than at our first meeting. She says she still feels drawn to him but no longer rushed.
Plan: she will keep her routines. Door open if anything changes.

qa.q: What did Parveen keep doing on Saturdays?
qa.a: She kept her Saturday badminton with her hostel friends.

qa.q: How does Parveen feel about Chinmay now?
qa.a: Parveen still feels drawn to Chinmay but no longer rushed; her laugh and less raised shoulders suggest she feels more at ease.

qa.q: What makes Parveen's approach a useful test?
qa.a: By asking for time and keeping friends and routines, Parveen can see how Chinmay handles a gentle no; staying warm, as he did after a day, is a good sign.

qa.q: How might Chinmay experience being asked to slow down?
qa.a: Chinmay might feel a sting of rejection at first, as his quiet day suggests, but asking about Sunday lunch shows he can stay warm when the pace changes.

grounding: Shows a young adult asking for time, keeping friends and routines, and watching how the other person handles a gentle no.
